organism: Haemophilus influenzae, a fastidious, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus. Encapsulated strains have a polysaccharide capsule in six antigenically distinct types (serotypes a-f); type b's capsule is polyribosyl-ribitol-phosphate (PRP), the polysaccharide used in Hib vaccines. In the prevaccine era, type b accounted for 95% of all invasive H. influenzae disease - there are currently no vaccines against the other encapsulated serotypes or nontypeable strains. The organism does not survive on inanimate surfaces.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: H. influenzae colonizes the nasopharynx, often asymptomatically, before occasionally invading the bloodstream and spreading to distant sites, especially the meninges. Incidence is strongly age-dependent, peaking at 6-11 months in the prevaccine era. The most common invasive presentations are meningitis (50%-65% of prevaccine cases, with a 3%-6% case fatality ratio and hearing impairment or other neurologic sequelae in 15%-30% of survivors), bacteremia, epiglottitis (which can cause life-threatening airway obstruction), pneumonia, arthritis, and cellulitis. Invasive disease generally requires hospitalization and about 10 days of antimicrobial therapy. Otitis media and bronchitis from H. influenzae are usually caused by nontypeable strains rather than type b.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only known reservoir. Transmission is person-to-person by inhalation of respiratory droplets or direct contact with respiratory secretions; neonates can also acquire it via amniotic fluid or genital tract contact during delivery. Prevaccine-era US data showed a bimodal seasonal pattern (September-December and March-May), though the reason is unclear. The contagious potential of invasive disease is generally limited, but close-contact settings (household, child care, institutional) can produce outbreaks or secondary transmission.
secularTrendsSummary: Before vaccination, about 20,000 cases occurred annually in the US, mostly in children under 5 (40-50 cases per 100,000). Incidence began declining dramatically in the late 1980s with conjugate vaccine licensure and has fallen more than 99% since the prevaccine era. In 2018, 38 cases of invasive Hib disease were reported nationally (about 0.08 per 100,000 among children under 5), against a backdrop of rising overall invasive H. influenzae disease (all serotypes combined, 1.23 to 2.08 per 100,000 from 1997 to 2018) driven by non-b and nontypeable strains that current vaccines don't target. Of 36 Hib cases in children under 5 reported 2009-2018, most were in children who were unvaccinated, undervaccinated, or too young to be vaccinated. Among children born 2016-2017, 92.2% had received the Hib primary series and 79.9% the full series (primary plus booster) by 24 months.
vaccineDescription: A polysaccharide-only vaccine (1985-1988) had poor immunogenicity in children under 2 and is no longer used. Conjugating the polysaccharide to a protein carrier (first licensed 1987) converts it to a T-dependent antigen, dramatically improving immunogenicity in young children and enabling a true booster response. Three monovalent conjugate vaccines are currently licensed: PRP-T (ActHIB, Hiberix), which uses a tetanus toxoid carrier, and PRP-OMP (PedvaxHIB), which uses a meningococcal outer membrane protein carrier and contains aluminum adjuvant. Hib is also included in two combination vaccines: DTaP-IPV/Hib (Pentacel, uses PRP-T) and DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB (Vaxelis, uses PRP-OMP). All are given by intramuscular injection.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: All infants begin a primary series at 2 months, but the number of doses depends on the specific product: PRP-T requires 3 primary doses (2, 4, 6 months), while PRP-OMP requires only 2 (2, 4 months) because it induces a protective response after the first dose. A booster follows at 12-15 months regardless of which product was used for the primary series, at least 8 weeks after the last primary dose. The recommended primary-series interval is 8 weeks, minimum 4 weeks; minimum age for dose 1 is 6 weeks. Monovalent Hib vaccines are interchangeable across brands, but Hib vaccine of any kind should never be given before 6 weeks of age, since earlier doses can induce immunologic tolerance and blunt the response to later doses.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Hib conjugate vaccines are highly immunogenic: more than 95% of infants develop protective antibody after a primary series, and clinical efficacy is estimated at 95%-100%. Invasive Hib disease is uncommon in fully vaccinated children. The vaccine is also immunogenic in high-risk patients (sickle-cell disease, leukemia, post-splenectomy), though immunogenicity in people with HIV varies with disease stage and degree of immunocompromise, and no efficacy studies have been done specifically in high-risk populations.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is age under 6 weeks (because of the immunologic-tolerance risk). Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. Combination vaccines containing Hib carry the contraindications of their individual components as well, which can differ by product.
vaccineSafetySummary: Adverse reactions are uncommon. Local reactions (swelling, redness, pain) occur in 5%-30% of recipients and usually resolve within 12-24 hours. Among VAERS reports following Hib vaccination, the most frequent adverse events were fever (31%), crying (11%), injection-site erythema (11%), irritability (10%), and rash (9%), with a median 1-day onset - reporting patterns are similar to other childhood vaccines, with no unusual safety signal identified. A Vaccine Safety Datalink study found children age 1-2 who received DTaP-IPV/Hib had an elevated risk of fever compared to a DTaP-only control, but no other associated adverse events.
vaccineStorageSummary: Hib vaccines must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Invasive H. influenzae infections became nationally notifiable in 1991, but reporting of serotype information (needed to distinguish vaccine-preventable type b from other serotypes) remains incomplete and varies by state. All H. influenzae isolates should be serotyped, especially from children under 15, since type b is the only serotype current vaccines target. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for case-definition and investigation guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Catch-Up Schedule for Previously Unvaccinated Children
supplementalTopics.summary: The number of catch-up doses needed depends on the child's age at the first dose and the product used. For PRP-T: age 2-6 months needs 3 doses 8 weeks apart plus a 12-15 month booster; age 7-11 months needs 2 doses 4 weeks apart plus a booster; age 12-14 months needs 1 dose plus a booster at least 8 weeks later; age 15-59 months needs only a single dose with no booster. For PRP-OMP, the pattern is the same except age 2-6 months needs only 2 doses (not 3) 8 weeks apart before the booster. In general, Hib vaccination of anyone older than 59 months is not recommended, since most older children are already immune from earlier asymptomatic exposure.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination of Special Populations and Older Children
supplementalTopics.summary: Children under 24 months who develop invasive Hib disease should still be vaccinated (starting during convalescence), since infection at that age does not reliably confer immunity. Children 12-59 months at elevated risk (chemotherapy, anatomic/functional asplenia including sickle-cell disease, HIV, immunoglobulin or early complement deficiency) need 2 additional doses 8 weeks apart if they received 0-1 dose before age 12 months, or 1 additional dose if they received 2 or more. Unimmunized persons 15 months or older facing elective splenectomy should get 1 dose at least 14 days beforehand; unimmunized people 5 or older with anatomic/functional asplenia, or children/adolescents 5-18 with HIV (adults with HIV do not need Hib vaccine), should get 1 dose. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients of any age should receive a fresh 3-dose series, 4 weeks apart, starting 6-12 months post-transplant, regardless of prior Hib vaccination history. For American Indian/Alaska Native infants - who have an earlier peak age of Hib meningitis - PRP-OMP is preferred for the primary series because it provides protection after just one dose.

keyPoints: Before vaccination, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children under 5; about 1 in 200 children in that age group developed invasive Hib disease

The first conjugate vaccine (1987) succeeded where the earlier polysaccharide-only vaccine (1985) failed, by converting a T-independent antigen into a T-dependent one - hugely improving immunogenicity in young children
The two licensed monovalent products require different numbers of primary doses (3 for PRP-T, 2 for PRP-OMP) because they use different carrier proteins with different immunogenicity in infancy
US Hib incidence has fallen more than 99% since the prevaccine era, even as overall invasive H. influenzae disease (all serotypes) has risen - non-b and nontypeable strains have no vaccine
All H. influenzae isolates should be serotyped, especially in children under 15, since type b is the only vaccine-preventable serotype
Never give Hib vaccine before 6 weeks of age - early doses can induce immunologic tolerance and blunt the response to later doses
